subject: Gaussian variance as a linear function of the mean

messages.author: 944a94c45996805c
messages.subject: Gaussian variance as a linear function of the mean
parts:
Hello,

I recently looked at some data where there was an obvious linear relationship between the mean and variance in a nested Gaussian model.  My initial attempts to model this relationship resulted in an enormous increase to warmup time and horrific ESS and Rhat figures.  For example the following simple model works well, 

data{
  int<lower=0> N_ ;   //number of data points e.g. N_ = 5000
  int<lower=0> n_b ;  //number of biologicaly unique proteins, e.g. n_b = 250
  int<lower=0, upper=n_b> bioID[N_] ; // Prot ID
  
  real lr[N_] ; //  observations

}

parameters{
  real<lower = 0> sigma; 
  real beta[n_b] ;
}

model{

  for( i in 1:n_b){
    beta[i] ~ normal(0,10);
  }
  
  sigma ~ normal(0,5)

  for(i in 1:N_){
    lr[i] ~ normal(beta[bioID[i]] , sigma ) ; 
  }

} // end model

However, just changing the distribution for the observations to 

      lr[i] ~ normal(beta[bioID[i]] ,  fabs(beta[bioID[i]])) ; 
    
or ideally to 

  lr[i] ~ normal(beta[bioID[i]] ,  fabs(beta[bioID[i]]) + sigma) ; 

causes substantial problems with the sampling.  
    
Does anyone have any suggestions for how this can be done more efficiently?  

Thanks,

Jonathon

messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Re: Gaussian variance as a linear function of the mean
parts:
Howdy Jonathon

My first question is, do you have a reason to believe your means and standard deviations should be linked like this in your model? Because if there isn't some higher level parameter you know about that you want to estimate, I think it'd be better to not code that in (cause you could be forcing a questionable model on your data). Rather, just give every group a mean and a sigma, and then look at the posteriors to figure out if there is a link or not.

My second is, if you estimate the means and variances of each group, you'll probably want to do some sort of hierarchical model so things don't go crazy. Have you seen these examples? There's the 8 schools one in BDA3, or Bob has some baseball examples (https://youtu.be/qQFF4tPgeWI?t=1h33m43s, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/pooling.html). 

Ben

Thanks for the suggestion!

In general, I agree that forcing the relationship will not be desirable.  However, I ran into a specific dataset where an exploratory analysis (just plotting group means against group sd's) was highly suggestive of a linear relationship.  So, I decided to play around and see if I could model it.  

Creating separate variance components for each group is problematic because the data is highly unbalanced with small sample sizes for many of the groups.  In general I'm happy with complete pooling, but a partial pooling model of the variance component is an interesting idea.  I'll give that a try.  

Do you expect that modeling the variance as a linear function of the mean is doomed to cause computational problems?

messages.subject: Re: Gaussian variance as a linear function of the mean
parts:
I'm not super familiar with modeling this, so maybe someone else can jump in. This sounds like something someone would have experience with.

Probly the easiest way to diagnose if a model is neurotic is some way (without digging into the math) is to just simulate data from the thing you're trying to fit, and then trying to fit it. Like, it's easy to generate data from a distribution normal(a/b, 1.0), but then trying to estimate 'a' and 'b' separately in a model is going to be hard (cause there are many 'a's and 'b's that are gonna give you good fits).

If Stan fits the simulated data easily, then the issue is probably something about the model not explaining your data very well that's causing your issues.

Hopefully that helps :D

Ben

Michael, thanks for sending me your exploration of divergence, it was very interesting.

Unfortunately, I'm still having a lot of trouble achieving convergence.  I tried specifying half-Cauchy(0,1) distributions and multiplying by cScale in the model.  Even with adapt_delta at .99 there were hundreds of divergent transitions. I then tried switching from half-Cauchy distributions to half-Normals.  This actually made things worse in terms of rhat and ess.   

So, I started to suspect that the problem might go beyond the geometry of the log-likelihood.  It turns out that the model with no pooling on the variance components also fails to converge.  Presumably, this is because many of the groups have only 1 or 2 data points making it impossible to estimate individual standard deviations.  In these cases I'm happy for the prior variance to be used, but maybe the difference in the scale of the prior is causing convergence problems?   

My current plan is to get the model with no pooling working before trying the hierarchical model again.  I'm hoping this can be done with the right selection of informative priors, but I'd be happy to hear any suggestions.

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: Gaussian variance as a linear function of the mean
parts:
Jonathon,

in your earlier post you use fabs:
lr[i] ~ normal(beta[bioID[i]] ,  fabs(beta[bioID[i]]) + sigma)

I first about using the log-likelihood of the normal distribution direct to used
a squared version, instead take the absolut.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution#Maximum_entropy

The mean parameter remains the same, your sigma has to be squared, eg. the variance.
You would avoid the fabs. Also the variances of the normal can be added,
in your example you added the parameter interpreted as SD. At least I would square and add
them and then take the sqrt.

 lr[i] ~ normal(beta[bioID[i]] ,  sqrt(square(beta[bioID[i]]) + square(sigma)))

A problem might be also the multi-modality, eg. square(sigma) and square(-sigma) leading to same.
Thus I think the constraint on sigma remain necessary. But what about square(beta[bioID[i]]))?

Andre

Ah, I see what you're saying.  Thanks Andre, I'll give that a try.  

Regarding the hierarchical model I finally got something to work.  Using a non-centered parameterization with either a half-Cauchy or half-Normal didn't seem to help (actually it might have made things worse).  However, with a non-centered Inverse-Gamma distribution (shape =1), I was able to reduce the divergent transitions to 7.  Increasing adapt-delta got rid of the rest of them.  

I still never managed to get the unpooled model to run without convergence problems.  I know it's a bad idea to begin with since many levels are highly dependent on the priors, but I'm surprised that it causes so much trouble.

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: Gaussian variance as a linear function of the mean
parts: You're right that a Gaussian model won't fit the data very well.  But I don't expect than anything will.  What you can see quite clearly in your plot is that a subset of the data appears to be coming from a totally different process.  Finding these clumps of data is one of the objectives we hope to achieve with our modeling efforts.

I would choose a skewed t-distribution, the skewness parameter to be positive with low degree of freedom
and another student-t and having a mixture distribution together with an mixture parameter for each bioID. 
 
Added:

This fits your group mean:

qqplot(tapply(lr,bioID,mean),rnorm(10000,0,0.5))

and skewed t-distribution fits your errors:

lrN <- lr-tapply(lr,bioID,mean)[bioID]
fit<-gamlss(lrN ~ 1,family=ST5())
qqplot(lrN,rST5(1000,-.0712,exp(-0.97),0.007,exp(0.28)))

Then we have:

means ~ normal(0, 0.5);
lr ~ ST5(means[bioID] -.0712,exp(-0.97),0.007,exp(0.28));

The ST5 is the skewed t-dist. from this forum.

Andre
